clause_heading: Conditions for a Hindu marriage
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 5 (Conditions for a Hindu marriage)

A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled: (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; (ii) at the time of the marriage, neither party is incapable of giving a valid consent in consequence of unsoundness of mind, or has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind as to be unfit for marriage, or subject to recurrent attacks of insanity; (iii) the bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride the age of eighteen years at the time of marriage; (iv) the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits; (v) the parties are not sapindas of each other, unless custom permits.

clause_heading: Divorce on fault grounds
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 13 (Divorce on fault grounds)

(1) Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, may, on a petition presented by either the husband or the wife, be dissolved by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other party - (ia) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, treated the petitioner with cruelty; or (ib) has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition; or (ii) has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion; or (iii) has been incurably of unsound mind; or (v) has been suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form. (2) A wife may also present a petition on grounds of husband bigamy or failure to comply with maintenance decree under Section 18 HAMA.

clause_heading: Divorce by mutual consent
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 13B (Divorce by mutual consent)

(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce may be presented to the district court by both the parties to a marriage together on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved. (2) On the motion of both the parties made not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition and not later than eighteen months, the court shall, on being satisfied after hearing the parties and making such inquiry as it thinks fit, pass a decree of divorce. Note: The 6-month statutory waiting period is directory and can be waived by the court where mediation has failed and settlement is complete (Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur).

clause_heading: Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 24 (Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings)

Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable. Application must be disposed of within sixty days from date of service of notice.

clause_heading: Permanent alimony and maintenance
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 25 (Permanent alimony and maintenance)

Any court exercising jurisdiction under this Act may, at the time of passing any decree or at any time subsequent thereto, on application made to it for the purpose by either the wife or the husband, order that the respondent shall pay to the applicant for her or his maintenance and support such gross sum or such monthly or periodical sum for a term not exceeding the life of the applicant as, having regard to the respondent's own income and other property, if any, the income and other property of the applicant, the conduct of the parties and other circumstances of the case, it may seem to the court to be just.

clause_heading: Devolution of interest in coparcenary property
chunk_text:
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 · Section 6 (Devolution of interest in coparcenary property)

(1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall: (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son. As affirmed in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), this right is conferred by birth and is not conditional upon the father being alive on September 9, 2005.

clause_heading: General rules of succession in the case of males
chunk_text:
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 · Section 8 (General rules of succession in the case of males)

The property of a male Hindu dying intestate shall devolve according to the provisions of this Chapter: (a) firstly, upon the heirs, being the relatives specified in Class I of the Schedule; (b) secondly, if there is no heir of Class I, then upon the relatives specified in Class II of the Schedule; (c) thirdly, if there is no heir of any of the two classes, then upon the agnates of the deceased; and (d) lastly, if there is no agnate, then upon the cognates of the deceased. Class I heirs include son, daughter, widow, mother, son/daughter of predeceased son, and specified issues.

clause_heading: Application of personal law to Muslims
chunk_text:
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 · Section 2 (Application of personal law to Muslims)

Notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary, in all questions regarding intestate succession, special property of females including personal property inherited or obtained under contract or gift or any other provision of Personal Law, marriage, dissolution of marriage including talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula and mubarat, maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts and trust properties, and waqfs, the rule of decision in cases where the parties are Muslims shall be the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat).

clause_heading: Grounds for decree for dissolution of marriage
chunk_text:
Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 · Section 2 (Grounds for decree for dissolution of marriage)

A woman married under Muslim law shall be entitled to obtain a decree for the dissolution of her marriage on any one or more of the following grounds: (i) that the whereabouts of the husband have not been known for a period of four years; (ii) that the husband has neglected or has failed to provide for her maintenance for a period of two years; (iii) that the husband has been sentenced to imprisonment for a period of seven years or upwards; (iv) that the husband has failed to perform, without reasonable cause, his marital obligations for a period of three years; (viii) that the husband treats her with cruelty (physical, emotional, or associates with women of evil repute).

act: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
clause_heading: Mahr and maintenance to be paid to divorced Muslim woman
chunk_text:
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 · Section 3 (Mahr and maintenance to be paid to divorced Muslim woman)

(1) A divorced woman shall be entitled to: (a) a reasonable and fair provision and maintenance to be made and paid to her within the iddat period by her former husband; (b) where she maintains children born before or after divorce, reasonable maintenance for two years from birth; (c) an amount equal to the sum of mahr or dower agreed to be paid to her at the time of marriage or after; (d) all the properties given to her before or at the time of marriage or after. Constitutional Interpretation: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740 settled that the husband must make 'reasonable and fair provision' within the iddat period which contemplates maintenance for her entire life until she remarries, not merely for the duration of iddat.

act: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019
clause_heading: Prohibition and punishment for Talaq-e-Biddat (Triple Talaq)
chunk_text:
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 · Section 3 & 4 (Prohibition and punishment for Talaq-e-Biddat (Triple Talaq))

Section 3: Any pronouncement of talaq by a Muslim husband upon his wife, by words, either spoken or written or in electronic form or in any other manner whatsoever, shall be void and illegal. Section 4: Any Muslim husband who pronounces talaq referred to in section 3 upon his wife shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. Section 5 & 6: Divorced wife is entitled to subsistence allowance and custody of minor children.

clause_heading: Conditions and notice of intended civil marriage
chunk_text:
Special Marriage Act, 1954 · Section 4 & 5 (Conditions and notice of intended civil marriage)

Section 4: A marriage between any two persons may be solemnized under this Act, if neither party has a spouse living; neither party is incapable of giving valid consent; male has completed 21 and female 18 years; and parties are not in prohibited relationship. Section 5: When a marriage is intended to be solemnized under this Act, the parties shall give notice thereof in writing in the form specified in the Second Schedule to the Marriage Officer of the district in which at least one of the parties has resided for not less than thirty days. The 30-day notice is published in the office of the Marriage Officer inviting objections under Section 7.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
clause_heading: Definition of domestic violence
chunk_text:
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 · Section 3 (Definition of domestic violence)

Domestic violence includes any act, omission or commission or conduct of the respondent that: (a) harms or injures or endangers the health, safety, life, limb or well-being, whether mental or physical, of the aggrieved person and includes causing physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, and economic abuse; or (b) harasses, harms, injures or endangers the aggrieved person with a view to coerce her or any other person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for dowry; or (c) has the effect of threatening the aggrieved person or any person related to her.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
clause_heading: Protection and Residence Orders in shared household
chapter: Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Reliefs
chunk_text:
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 · Section 18 & 19 (Protection and Residence Orders in shared household)

Section 18: Magistrate may pass a protection order prohibiting respondent from committing any domestic violence, aiding or abetting, entering workplace of aggrieved person, attempting to communicate, alienating assets, or causing violence to dependents. Section 19: Magistrate may pass a residence order restraining respondent from dispossessing aggrieved person from shared household, directing respondent to remove himself from shared household, or directing respondent to secure same level of alternate accommodation and pay rent for the same.

act: Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022
clause_heading: Prohibition of unlawful conversion and penalty
chunk_text:
Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022 · Section 3 & 5 (Prohibition of unlawful conversion and penalty)

Section 3: No person shall convert or attempt to convert, either directly or otherwise, any other person from one religion to another by use of misrepresentation, force, undue influence, coercion, allurement or by any fraudulent means or by marriage, nor shall any person abet or conspire for such conversion. Section 5: Any person who contravenes the provisions of section 3 shall be punished with imprisonment for a term of three to five years and fine. If conversion involves a minor, woman, or SC/ST person, imprisonment shall be three to ten years. Section 6: Any marriage which was done for the sole purpose of unlawful conversion shall be declared null and void by the Family Court.

clause_heading: Documents compulsorily registrable and effect of non-registration
chunk_text:
Registration Act, 1908 · Section 17 & 49 (Documents compulsorily registrable and effect of non-registration)

Section 17: Documents of which registration is compulsory include instruments of gift of immovable property, other non-testamentary instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards in immovable property, and leases exceeding one year. Section 49: No document required by section 17 to be registered shall affect any immovable property comprised therein, or be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property, unless it has been registered.

clause_heading: Execution under power-of-attorney and limitation on title transfer
chunk_text:
Powers-of-Attorney Act, 1882 · Section 2 (Execution under power-of-attorney and limitation on title transfer)

The donee of a power-of-attorney may, if he thinks fit, execute or do any assurance, instrument or thing in and with his own name and signature by the authority of the donor. Supreme Court Principle (Suraj Lamp v. State of Haryana (2012) 1 SCC 656): A General Power of Attorney (GPA) is merely an agency authorization. A GPA, Agreement to Sell, or Living Will does NOT transfer title or create ownership interest in immovable property. Ownership can be transferred solely through a duly stamped and registered Deed of Conveyance (Sale Deed) under TPA Section 54.

clause_heading: Recovery of specific immovable property and summary suit
chunk_text:
Specific Relief Act, 1963 · Section 5 & 6 (Recovery of specific immovable property and summary suit)

Section 5: A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Section 6: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. Limitation: Suit under Section 6 must be brought within six months from the date of dispossession, and no suit lies against the Government.

clause_heading: Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right and perpetual injunction
chunk_text:
Specific Relief Act, 1963 · Section 34 & 38 (Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right and perpetual injunction)

Section 34: Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may make therein a declaration that he is so entitled. Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief (possession), omits to do so. Section 38: Perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favor of the applicant. Ruling (Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy): Where plaintiff title is in dispute or under cloud and he is not in possession, suit for bare injunction does not lie; suit must be filed for declaration of title with consequential recovery of possession.

clause_heading: Uses of agricultural land and procedure for diversion for non-agricultural purpose
chapter: Use of Land and Revenue Exemptions
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 95 (Uses of agricultural land and procedure for diversion for non-agricultural purpose)

(1) An occupant of land assessed or held for the purpose of agriculture is entitled by himself, his servants, tenants, agents, or other legal representatives to erect farm buildings, construct wells or tanks, or make any other improvements thereon for the better cultivation of the land. (2) If any occupant of land assessed or held for agriculture wishes to divert such land or any part thereof to any other purpose (residential, commercial, industrial), he shall apply for permission to the Deputy Commissioner who may, subject to the provisions of this section and rules made thereunder, grant permission on terms. Where master plan exists under Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, conversion operates under simplified deemed approval upon payment of statutory conversion fees.

clause_heading: Record of rights (RTC/Pahani) and acquisition of rights to be reported
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 127 & 128 (Record of rights (RTC/Pahani) and acquisition of rights to be reported)

Section 127: A Record of Rights (Pahani / RTC Form 16) shall be maintained in every village containing survey numbers, area, names of holders, cultivators, nature of tenure, rent, liabilities, and government water cess. Section 128: Any person acquiring by succession, survivorship, inheritance, partition, purchase, gift or otherwise, any right as holder, occupant, or mortgagee of land shall report orally or in writing his acquisition of such right to the village accountant within three months from date of acquisition. If acquired under registered deed, Sub-Registrar automatically transmits intimation (J-Slip) to Revenue authorities on Bhoomi.

clause_heading: Registration of mutations and appeal against revenue orders
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 129 & 136 (Registration of mutations and appeal against revenue orders)

Section 129: The Village Accountant enters every report in a register of mutations and posts a copy in the chavadi inviting objections within thirty days. If contested, the matter is registered in the register of disputed cases (Form 12) and enquired into by the Tahsildar. Section 136: Any person aggrieved by an entry or mutation order of the Tahsildar may prefer an appeal to the Assistant Commissioner within sixty days (Sec 136(2)). The Deputy Commissioner may call for records and examine legality under revision powers (Sec 136(3)). Legal Nature: Supreme Court settled (Jitendra Singh (2021)) that mutation entries in revenue records are for fiscal taxation purposes only; they do NOT confer or extinguish title. Title disputes belong exclusively to Civil Courts.

clause_heading: Determination of village and field boundaries (Phodi and Durasti)
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 140 (Determination of village and field boundaries (Phodi and Durasti))

The boundaries of villages and fields shall be determined and demarcated with boundary marks by survey officers. Where a survey number is sub-divided (partition or sale of fraction of agricultural holding), a Phodi survey must be conducted to carve out independent Hissa numbers and prepare a sub-division survey sketch (Tippani). Durasti is the official revenue process of rectifying boundary anomalies or missing boundary stones to match ground possession with land records.

act: Karnataka SC & ST (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978
clause_heading: Prohibition of transfer of granted lands and resumption by Assistant Commissioner
chunk_text:
Karnataka SC & ST (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 · Section 4 & 5 (Prohibition of transfer of granted lands and resumption by Assistant Commissioner)

Section 4: (1) Notwithstanding anything in any law, agreement, contract or instrument, any transfer of granted land made either before or after the commencement of this Act, in contravention of the terms of grant or without previous permission of the Government, shall be null and void and no right, title or interest in such land shall be conveyed or deemed ever to have conveyed by such transfer. Section 5: The Assistant Commissioner may, on application by any interested person or on information, by order declare transfer void, evict the purchaser, resume the granted land to Government, and restore it to the original grantee or their legal heirs. Limitation: Supreme Court held in Nekkanti Rama Lakshmi (2020) that PTCL restoration must be initiated within a reasonable time (typically 10-15 years); inordinate unexplained delay of decades disentitles resumption.

clause_heading: Property tax self-assessment and unauthorized building regulation
chunk_text:
Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike Act, 2020 · Section 144 & 313 (Property tax self-assessment and unauthorized building regulation)

Section 144: Property tax is levied on all lands and buildings within BBMP limits on the basis of Unit Area Value (UAV) under Self-Assessment Scheme (SAS). A-Khata is issued for properties in layouts approved by BDA, BMRDA, or BBMP with converted land. B-Khata is an entry in the property tax collection register maintained under Section 108A KMC Act / BBMP Act for properties with building deviations, unapproved layouts, or un-converted revenue sites; B-Khata acknowledges payment of property tax but does NOT grant building sanction or legal title. Section 313 & 321: Building construction without prior sanction or in violation of building bylaws is subject to provisional notice, confirmation order, and demolition, and no Occupancy Certificate shall be issued for deviated structures.

clause_heading: Formation of co-operative society or association and conveyance of title
chunk_text:
Karnataka Ownership Flats Act, 1972 · Section 10 & 11 (Formation of co-operative society or association and conveyance of title)

Section 10: As soon as a minimum number of persons required, or sixty percent of flat purchasers, have taken possession of flats, the promoter shall submit an application to the Registrar for registration of the organization of flat owners as a co-operative housing society or an association of flat owners under the Karnataka Apartment Ownership Act, 1972. Section 11: A promoter shall take all necessary steps to complete his title and execute a conveyance deed transferring the land, common areas, and undivided share in favour of the registered association of flat owners within the prescribed period.

act: Karnataka Gram Swaraj and Panchayat Raj Act, 1993
clause_heading: Property tax levy in Gram Panchayat limits and e-Swathu system
chunk_text:
Karnataka Gram Swaraj and Panchayat Raj Act, 1993 · Section 199 (Property tax levy in Gram Panchayat limits and e-Swathu system)

Gram Panchayats levy property tax on buildings and lands situated within their territorial jurisdiction. Under the Government of Karnataka e-Swathu software system, two statutory digital forms are generated: 1. Form 9: Extract from the Village Site Property Register (Gramathana property), certifying the plot is situated inside original settlement limits. 2. Form 11: Extract from the Property Tax Demand and Collection Register for properties situated outside old gramathana that have valid conversion orders. Mandate: Sub-Registrars in Karnataka are strictly barred from registering any deed of transfer of rural site without a digitally verified Form 9 and Form 11.

act: FEMA (Acquisition and Transfer of Immovable Property in India) Regulations, 2018
clause_heading: Acquisition and transfer of property in India by NRI and OCI
chunk_text:
FEMA (Acquisition and Transfer of Immovable Property in India) Regulations, 2018 · Regulation 3 & 4 (Acquisition and transfer of property in India by NRI and OCI)

Regulation 3: A Non-Resident Indian (NRI) or an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) may acquire any immovable property in India other than agricultural land, farm house, or plantation property. Payment for acquisition must be made out of funds received in India through normal banking channels by inward remittance or debit to NRE/FCNR(B)/NRO account of the person. Regulation 4: An NRI or OCI may transfer any immovable property in India to a person resident in India, or transfer non-agricultural property to an NRI or OCI. Sale proceeds may be repatriated abroad up to USD 1,000,000 per financial year subject to payment of applicable capital gains taxes.

clause_heading: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 318 (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property)

Defines cheating as fraudulently or dishonestly deceiving any person to deliver property or consent to retain property. Sub-section (4) covers cheating with dishonest inducement to deliver property or alter valuable securities, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine (formerly Section 420 IPC).

clause_heading: Theft and community service for petty theft
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 303 (Theft and community service for petty theft)

Defines theft as dishonestly taking movable property out of the possession of any person without consent. Sub-section (2) provides punishment of imprisonment up to three years, fine, or both. For first-time petty theft involving stolen property valued below five thousand rupees upon return, community service may be ordered.

clause_heading: Cruelty to a woman by husband or relatives
chapter: Chapter V: Offences Against Women and Children
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 85 & 86 (Cruelty to a woman by husband or relatives)

Section 85 penalizes a husband or his relative who subjects a woman to cruelty with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Section 86 defines cruelty as conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury, or harassment to coerce her or her relatives into meeting unlawful property demands (formerly Section 498A IPC).

clause_heading: Information in cognizable cases and Zero FIR procedure
chapter: Chapter XIII: Information to the Police and Powers to Investigate
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 173 (Information in cognizable cases and Zero FIR procedure)

Mandates registration of an FIR for any cognizable offence, irrespective of jurisdictional area (Zero FIR). Permits electronic communication of information, requiring informant signature within three days. In offences punishable with three to seven years imprisonment, preliminary inquiry may be conducted within fourteen days with prior permission of a Deputy Superintendent of Police before proceeding.

clause_heading: Procedure and limits on police arrest
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 35 (Procedure and limits on police arrest)

Specifies when police may arrest without warrant. For offences punishable with up to seven years imprisonment, arrest requires recorded satisfaction of necessity grounds (preventing tampering, absconding, further offences). Sub-section (3) mandates issuance of a notice of appearance where arrest is not deemed necessary (formerly Section 41A CrPC).

clause_heading: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest
chapter: Chapter XXXV: Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 482 (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest)

Empowers the High Court and Sessions Court to grant anticipatory bail to any person apprehending arrest in non-bailable offences. Evaluates nature and gravity of accusation, criminal antecedents, possibility of fleeing justice, and whether accusations appear motivated to humiliate the applicant (formerly Section 438 CrPC).

clause_heading: Admissibility of electronic records and certification
chapter: Chapter V: Documentary and Electronic Evidence
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 · Section 63 (Admissibility of electronic records and certification)

Provides that information contained in an electronic record printed, stored, or copied in optical/magnetic media shall be deemed an admissible document without proof of original, provided statutory conditions of system integrity are met. Requires an accompanying certificate signed by the person in lawful management or an authorized official (formerly Section 65B IEA).

clause_heading: Victim compensation scheme and legal services authority awards
chapter: Chapter XXIX: Judgment and Victim Rights
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 396 (Victim compensation scheme and legal services authority awards)

Directs State Governments in coordination with Central Government to maintain victim compensation funds. The trial court may recommend compensation to District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or State Legal Services Authority (SLSA). Enables award of interim medical and rehabilitative relief to victims of rape, acid attack, and severe trauma, even where the offender is not identified or convicted (formerly Section 357A CrPC).

clause_heading: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds and procedure
chapter: Chapter XVII: Penalties in Case of Dishonour of Cheques
chunk_text:
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Section 138 & 142 (Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds and procedure)

Penalizes dishonour of a cheque drawn for discharge of legally enforceable debt with imprisonment up to two years, fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. Prescribes strict timelines: statutory written demand notice must be dispatched within thirty days of cheque return memo; the drawer has fifteen days to settle payment; failing which a complaint must be filed before the Judicial Magistrate First Class within thirty days under Section 142.

clause_heading: Enforcement of security interest without court intervention
chapter: Chapter III: Enforcement of Security Interest
chunk_text:
SARFAESI Act, 2002 · Section 13 (Enforcement of security interest without court intervention)

Allows secured creditor banks to enforce security interests upon Non-Performing Asset (NPA) classification. Section 13(2) mandates sixty days notice to discharge liabilities in full. Under Section 13(3A), the borrower may submit representations which the creditor must decide within fifteen days. Upon default, Section 13(4) empowers the bank to take symbolic or physical possession of the secured asset, challengeable before the DRT under Section 17 within forty-five days.

clause_heading: Borrower safeguards, KFS, and prohibition on recovery harassment
chunk_text:
RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending, 2022 · Regulatory Directions (Borrower safeguards, KFS, and prohibition on recovery harassment)

Mandates direct loan disbursement and repayment between borrower bank account and Regulated Entity without third-party pooling. Requires delivery of a standardized Key Fact Statement (KFS) stating All-Inclusive Annual Percentage Rate (APR). Enforces a look-up/cooling-off exit window without prepayment penalties. Strictly forbids loan recovery agents from accessing borrower contacts, location, media files, or making threatening and unauthorized communication.

clause_heading: Consumer rights, electronic e-Daakhil filing, and two-year limitation
chapter: Chapter IV: Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
chunk_text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 · Section 2(7), 35 & 69 (Consumer rights, electronic e-Daakhil filing, and two-year limitation)

Defines a consumer as any person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, excluding commercial resale. Section 35 enables filing complaints before the District Consumer Commission online through e-Daakhil. Section 69 prescribes a two-year limitation period from the date of the cause of action. Provides remedies including refund, replacement, removal of defects, and compensation for deficiency in service or product liability.

act: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
clause_heading: Prohibited deceptive digital interface practices in e-commerce
chunk_text:
CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 · Guidelines 4 & 5 (Prohibited deceptive digital interface practices in e-commerce)

Prohibits thirteen specified dark pattern techniques used on platforms, including False Urgency (fabricated countdown timers), Basket Sneaking (adding unselected items or donations into cart), Subscription Traps (deliberately obstructing cancellation of recurring memberships), and Drip Pricing (revealing mandatory fees only at final checkout). Actionable as unfair trade practices.

clause_heading: Gratuity eligibility, computation formula, and payment timeline
chunk_text:
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 · Section 4 & 7 (Gratuity eligibility, computation formula, and payment timeline)

Section 4 grants gratuity to an employee upon termination after completing five years of continuous service (waived on death or disablement). Calculated at fifteen days wages per completed service year based on last drawn basic and DA. Section 7 requires the employer to disburse gratuity within thirty days of it becoming payable, failing which simple interest at the notified rate is mandatory.

act: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
clause_heading: Mandatory Internal Committee and complaint procedure
chunk_text:
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 · Section 4 & 9 (Mandatory Internal Committee and complaint procedure)

Section 4 mandates constitution of an Internal Committee (IC) in every workplace employing ten or more persons, headed by a senior woman employee with an external NGO member. Section 9 permits aggrieved women to file a complaint within three months of incident (extendable by three months). Inquiries must be completed within ninety days with interim protections.

clause_heading: Patient rights, rate disclosure, and dead body retention prohibition
chunk_text:
Karnataka Private Medical Establishments Act, 2007 · Patient Charter & Pricing (Patient rights, rate disclosure, and dead body retention prohibition)

Mandates registration and quality standards for all private clinics, diagnostic centres, and hospitals in Karnataka. Requires prominent display of package rates and medical fee schedules. Explicitly prohibits medical establishments from detaining the body of a deceased patient on grounds of unpaid hospital charges or outstanding billing disputes. Establishes District Grievance Redressal Committees to investigate medical complaints.

clause_heading: Capital gains taxation on property sale and 1% TDS requirement
chapter: Chapter IV: Capital Gains & Chapter XVII: Collection and Recovery
chunk_text:
Income-tax Act, 1961 · Section 45, 54 & 194-IA (Capital gains taxation on property sale and 1% TDS requirement)

Section 45 charges profits from the transfer of a capital asset (such as immovable property) to capital gains tax. Section 54 provides tax exemption for individuals if long-term capital gains from residential property sale are reinvested in purchasing or constructing a new residential house within statutory timelines. Section 194-IA mandates the buyer to deduct 1% TDS on the total sale consideration if the property transaction value is fifty lakh rupees or higher.

act: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006
clause_heading: Mandatory payment window and compound interest on delayed MSME payments
chapter: Chapter V: Delayed Payments to Micro and Small Enterprises
chunk_text:
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 · Section 15, 16 & 18 (Mandatory payment window and compound interest on delayed MSME payments)

Section 15 requires buyers to pay suppliers within agreed timelines not exceeding forty-five days from delivery. Section 16 penalizes delayed payments with compound interest with monthly rests at three times the RBI bank rate. Section 18 permits MSMEs to file references before the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFC Samadhaan portal) for conciliation and binding arbitration. An appeal requires 75% pre-deposit under Section 19.

clause_heading: Disposal of requests and emergency life or liberty timeline
chapter: Chapter II: Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
chunk_text:
Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 7 (Disposal of requests and emergency life or liberty timeline)

Directs the Public Information Officer (PIO) to provide requested information or reject it with reasons within thirty days of receipt of application. Where the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person, it must be provided within forty-eight hours. Failure to respond within the stipulated period constitutes a deemed refusal, entitling the applicant to file a First Appeal under Section 19(1).

act: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
clause_heading: Free compulsory education and 25% quota in private unaided schools
chapter: Right to Free and Compulsory Education
chunk_text:
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 · Section 3, 12 & 13 (Free compulsory education and 25% quota in private unaided schools)

Section 3 guarantees every child aged six to fourteen years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighborhood school. Section 12(1)(c) mandates private unaided schools to admit at least twenty-five percent children belonging to economically weaker and disadvantaged groups in class I. Section 13 strictly prohibits schools from collecting capitation fees or subjecting children and parents to screening interviews.

clause_heading: Punishment for identity theft and cheating by personation using computer resource
chunk_text:
Information Technology Act, 2000 · Section 66C & 66D (Punishment for identity theft and cheating by personation using computer resource)

Section 66C punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Section 66D penalizes cheating by personation over computer systems or telecommunication devices (phishing, OTP fraud, spoofing) with imprisonment up to three years and fine.

clause_heading: Driving by a drunken person or by a person under the influence of drugs
chapter: Chapter XIII: Offences, Penalties and Procedure
chunk_text:
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Section 185 (Driving by a drunken person or by a person under the influence of drugs)

Whoever, while driving, or attempting to drive, a motor vehicle - (a) has, in his blood, alcohol exceeding 30 mg. per 100 ml. of blood detected in a test by a breath analyser, or in any other test including a laboratory test, or (b) is under the influence of a drug to such an extent as to be incapable of exercising proper control over the vehicle, shall be punishable for the first offence with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine of ten thousand rupees, or with both; and for a second or subsequent offence, if committed within three years of the commission of the previous similar offence, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine of fifteen thousand rupees, or with both. The driving licence of the offender is also liable to suspension or disqualification by the licensing authority.

clause_heading: Penalties for traffic violations, helmet, seatbelt, and compounding of offences
chapter: Chapter XIII: Offences, Penalties and Procedure
chunk_text:
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Section 194 & Section 200 (Penalties for traffic violations, helmet, seatbelt, and compounding of offences)

Section 194B prescribes a penalty of one thousand rupees for driving without wearing a safety belt. Section 194C and 194D prescribe a penalty of one thousand rupees for riding without protective headgear (helmet) and three months disqualification of licence. Section 184 penalizes dangerous or rash driving with fines up to five thousand rupees. Section 200 authorizes designated police and transport officers to compound specified traffic offences on the spot or through electronic virtual courts / e-challan systems. When compounding a traffic fine, police officers must issue an official electronic or physical printed receipt. A citizen has the legal right to challenge an erroneous traffic challan before the designated Metropolitan Magistrate or Virtual Court.

clause_heading: Form of summons, service of summons on person, and notice of appearance
chapter: Chapter VI: Processes to Compel Appearance
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 63 & Section 64 (Form of summons, service of summons on person, and notice of appearance)

Every summons issued by a Court under BNSS shall be in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer or designated officer, and bear the seal of the Court. The summons may be served by a police officer, an officer of the court, or electronically via encrypted electronic communication. Service is effected by tendering or delivering a duplicate copy to the person summoned. Under Section 35 BNSS, a police officer where arrest is not mandatory may issue a formal written notice of appearance to any person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made. When a citizen receives a court summons, they must examine whether they are summoned as a witness or as an accused, note the exact court room, case number, and appearance date, and appear in person or through an empanelled advocate to prevent issuance of bailable or non-bailable warrants.

clause_heading: Acquisition of rights, reporting of plot ownership change, and mutation register
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 128 & Section 129 (Acquisition of rights, reporting of plot ownership change, and mutation register)

Section 128 requires any person acquiring by succession, survivorship, inheritance, partition, purchase, mortgage, gift or otherwise, any right in any land or plot, to report orally or in writing his acquisition of such right to the prescribed revenue officer (Village Accountant or Tahsildar / Bhoomi portal) within three months from the date of such acquisition. Section 129 mandates the revenue officer to enter the acquisition in the Register of Mutations (Form 12) and post a copy at the village chavadi, issuing notice to all persons interested. If no objection is received within thirty days, the mutation is certified and the RTC / Pahani is updated. For urban plots under BBMP or municipal corporations, change of plot ownership requires submitting the registered Sale Deed, Encumbrance Certificate, and previous tax receipts to secure an e-Khata or A-Khata transfer under Section 114 of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act.

clause_heading: Summons to defendant to appear and answer plaint, and 30-day written statement limit
chunk_text:
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 · Order V Rule 1 & Rule 9 (Summons to defendant to appear and answer plaint, and 30-day written statement limit)

When a civil suit has been duly instituted, a summons may be issued to the defendant to appear and answer the claim on a day specified therein. The defendant shall, within thirty days from the date of service of summons on him, present a written statement of his defence. Such period may be extended up to ninety days by the Court for reasons to be recorded in writing. Service of civil summons may be made by personal delivery, registered post acknowledgment due (RPAD), speed post, or authorized courier service.

act: Danial Latifi v. Union of India
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Danial Latifi v. Union of India
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Danial Latifi v. Union of India · (2001) 7 SCC 740
Court: Supreme Court of India (Constitution Bench) | Date of Decision: 2001-09-28

ISSUE:
Does a Muslim husband liability to maintain his divorced wife terminate at the end of the iddat period under the 1986 Act?

HOLDING:
A Muslim husband must make reasonable and fair provision within the iddat period that contemplates maintenance for the woman entire lifetime until remarriage.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Interpreting Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act to conform with Articles 14 and 21, the liability is not limited to iddat period expenses; reasonable provision must be made to sustain the woman throughout her life.

act: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab · (2005) 6 SCC 1
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2005-08-05

ISSUE:
What standard of negligence is required to sustain a criminal prosecution against a medical professional?

HOLDING:
Criminal liability requires proof of gross negligence or recklessness. An FIR should not be registered against a doctor without obtaining an independent qualified medical opinion.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
A simple lack of care or error of judgment does not constitute criminal rashness under Section 304A IPC / Section 106 BNS; the degree of negligence must be gross and accompanied by reckless disregard for patient safety.

act: Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni · (2020) 10 SCC 783
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2020-11-02

ISSUE:
Does the enactment of RERA bar a homebuyer from approaching the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission?

HOLDING:
Remedies under the Consumer Protection Act and RERA are concurrent; a homebuyer may initiate proceedings before Consumer Forums notwithstanding RERA.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Section 79 RERA bars civil courts, but Consumer Commissions are not civil courts. The remedies are cumulative, giving homebuyers freedom of forum choice for delayed project possession.

act: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar · (2014) 8 SCC 273
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2014-07-02

ISSUE:
Are police authorized to make automatic arrests in dowry harassment and offences punishable with up to seven years imprisonment?

HOLDING:
Police shall not automatically arrest accused persons in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years without complying with statutory checklists.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Arrest must not be made merely on the registration of a cognizable case. The investigating officer must issue a notice of appearance unless necessity grounds under Section 41 CrPC / Section 35 BNSS are satisfied and recorded.

act: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh · 2021 SCC OnLine SC 802
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2021-09-06

ISSUE:
Does a mutation entry in revenue records confer or extinguish legal title to immovable property?

HOLDING:
Mutation of property in revenue records neither creates nor extinguishes title, nor does it have any presumptive value on title.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Revenue records (Khata, RTC, Pahani) are maintained solely for fiscal collection purposes. If there is a dispute regarding title, the parties must seek relief before the competent Civil Court.

clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka · (1984) 3 SCC 301
Court: Supreme Court of India (Constitution Bench) | Date of Decision: 1984-04-17

ISSUE:
Is the Karnataka PTCL Act prohibiting alienation of granted land to SC/ST persons constitutionally valid?

HOLDING:
Upheld the constitutional validity of the PTCL Act as reasonable state affirmative action protecting vulnerable landless grantees.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Transfers of granted lands made in violation of grant conditions or statutory non-alienation clauses are void ab initio, and the State is empowered to resume and restore such lands without compensation to unauthorized purchasers.

act: Nekkanti Rama Lakshmi v. State of Karnataka
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Nekkanti Rama Lakshmi v. State of Karnataka
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Nekkanti Rama Lakshmi v. State of Karnataka · (2020) 14 SCC 232
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2017-10-26

ISSUE:
Can an application for resumption of granted land under Section 5 PTCL Act be entertained after an inordinate delay of several decades?

HOLDING:
Applications for resumption of land under the PTCL Act must be filed within a reasonable period; an unexplained delay of 25 years bars statutory relief.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Where no period of limitation is prescribed by statute, power must be exercised within a reasonable time. Rights settled over decades cannot be reopened arbitrarily to prejudice established possessory interests.

clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan · (2010) 11 SCC 441
Court: Supreme Court of India (3-Judge Bench) | Date of Decision: 2010-05-07

ISSUE:
Does the statutory presumption under Section 139 NI Act include the existence of a legally enforceable debt?

HOLDING:
The presumption mandated by Section 139 NI Act includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
The burden rests on the accused drawer to rebut the presumption by raising a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities; bare denial is insufficient.
